## Methods

Study site and experimental design
The study was conducted in the Changbai Mountain National Nature Reserve, located in Jilin Province in northern China (42.70° N,127.63° E). The region has a typical temperate climate, with a mean annual temperature of 3.6 ℃ and mean annual precipitation of 745 mm. The predominant coniferous species in the forest is Pinus koraiensis and the broad-leaved species are Quercus mongolica, Tilia amurensis, and Fraxinus mandshurica. The soils are Albic Luvisols developed from volcanic ash61. In October 2017, approximately 10 kg of fresh leaf litter from the forest floor, primarily consisting of Pinus koraiensis, Quercus mongolica, Fraxinus mandshurica, Tilia amurensis Rupr., and Asophora japonica Linn., was collected, dried, ground, and sterilized to use as the organic matter for building the model soils.

In May 2018, nine experimental plots (3 m × 3 m) were randomly established with > 5 m buffer zones between adjacent plots. Six soil cores (5 cm in diameter, 20 cm in depth) were randomly collected from each plot after removing the litter layer. The cores were combined into one composite sample, immediately transported to the laboratory on ice, and homogenized for microbial inoculum extraction.

We created low-clay, medium-clay, and high-clay model soils with 20%, 40%, and 60% clay content, respectively, using quartz sand, montmorillonite, and plant litter (Fig. 1). The model soils were placed in PVC tubes (5 cm in diameter and 14 cm in height) with closed bottoms using PVC pipe caps, inoculated with the microbial inoculum, and pre-incubated for 120 days in the laboratory62. After pre-incubation, the PVC tubes were installed in the experimental plots for a stabilization period of 30 days. Subsequently, 13C15N-labelled bacterial and fungal necromass were injected into the model soils as tracers and incubated for 386 days under in situ conditions (Fig. 1). The experiment consisted of nine treatments: either (a) with 13C15N-labelled bacterial necromass, (b) 13C15N-labelled fungal necromass, or (c) without necromass (controls were injected with water-only); each of which was applied to soils of three different clay contents (low, medium, and high). In each of the 6 necromass plots, 15 PVC tubes with bacterial or fungal necromass were installed, while in each of the 3 control plots, 7 PVC tubes without added necromass were installed, resulting in a total of 111 PVC tubes.

Preparation of model soils
The quartz sand (composed of 30% silt- and 70% sand-sized particles; sourced from Aladdin) was cleaned in diluted acid and combusted at 500 ℃ to remove organic carbon and then was ground and sieved to fine (50-250 μm) and coarse (250-2000 μm) particle sizes. Detailed properties of the model soil materials are listed in Table S9. A typical expandable 2:1 phyllosilicate clay (montmorillonite; sourced from Sigma-Aldrich) was mixed with quartz sand in varying proportions to form low-clay soil (sandy loam soil; 20% clay, 24% fine quartz, and 56% coarse quartz), medium-clay soil (clay loam soil; 40% clay, 18% fine quartz and 42% coarse quartz) and high-clay soil (clay soil; 60% clay, 12% fine quartz and 28% coarse quartz). The organic matter obtained from the forest dried leaf litter was mixed at 45 mg g-1 model soil. The specific surface area of the low, medium, and high-clay soil was 27.1, 59.1, and 94.9 m2 g−1 soil, respectively. The water holding capacity (WHC) of low-, medium- and high-clay soil was 0.60, 0.89, and 1.21, respectively, and increased significantly with clay content (Table S10).

Approximately 80 g of the model soil was placed in a PVC tube (5 cm in diameter, 14 cm in height) for each sample. The height and bulk density of the model soils were ~5.5 cm and 0.75 g cm−3, respectively. A total of 37 samples were prepared for each clay treatment. We created the microbial inoculum by suspending 10 g of the field-collected soil in 90 mL of deionized water46. After 3 days, each sample was inoculated with the microbial inoculum. All samples were pre-incubated at 20 ℃ and 60% WHC for 120 days to establish stable soil structure and microbial community. Litter water extract was added biweekly (1.4 mg C, 0.027 mg N g−1 soil). The litter water extract was created by mixing 150 g dried forest leaf litter with 2 L of deionized water and shaking for 24 h before filtering63.

Preparation of labelled microbial necromass
The 13C15N-labelled bacterial and fungal necromass was prepared by cultivating the microbial inoculum in a minimal M9 salts medium with 99 atom% 13C-glucose and 99.5 atom% 15NH4Cl in a rotary shaker incubator. The bacterial culture was grown in 500 mL batches for 3 days at 37 °C with the addition of a fungal inhibitor (cycloheximide). The fungal culture was grown in 500 mL batches for 4 weeks at 28 °C with the addition of bacterial inhibitors (ampicillin and streptomycin). The bacterial and fungal cultures were then collected by centrifugation, sterilized by ultraviolet irradiation, mixed thoroughly, and ground to powder. This approach yielded bacterial and fungal necromass with a much broader species composition than necromass generated from pure cultures. The atom % 13C and atom % 15N of microbial necromass exceeded 71.95% and 92.08%, respectively (Table S1). The phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) analysis confirmed that bacterial necromass predominantly consisted of bacterial species, while fungal necromass predominantly consisted of fungal species (Table S11).

Field experiment with dual-labelled microbial necromass
After laboratory pre-incubation of the model soils, on 19 August 2018, the PVC tubes were transported to the established field plots. Plots were randomly assigned to each treatment. In each necromass plot, we first filled the top ~8.5 cm of the PVC tubes with natural subsoils (5.5-14 cm), then turned the PVC tubes over and removed the PVC caps. We then inserted 15 PVC tubes of the same clay treatment into the soil to a depth of 14 cm after removing the natural soil. During the experiment, both ends of the PVC tubes were open, and the model soils were separated from the surrounding natural soil by a 1 mm nylon mesh, which allowed physical contact while preventing direct mixing. In each control plot, 7 PVC tubes were installed using the same process. The PVC tubes were placed in the plots for about one month prior to the addition of necromass to minimize potential disturbance effects associated with long-distance transport of the model soils.

On 18 September 2018, the necromass (10 mg dry weight) was suspended in deionized water and injected with a side-port needle in a 10-point grid pattern at a depth of 3 cm in the model soils within the PVC tubes. The added microbial necromass corresponded to an average of 9% and 22% of model soil C and N, respectively. Within each necromass plot, 15 PVC tubes were injected either with 13C15N-labelled bacterial or fungal necromass, while in each control plot, 7 PVC tubes were injected with deionized water.

Three PVC tubes with bacterial necromass or three PVC tubes with fungal necromass from each necromass plot, and one control PVC tube from each control plot were collected on 28 September 2018 (10 days), 18 October 2018 (30 days), 24 April 2019 (218 days) and 9 October 2019 (386 days). The soils from the collected PVC tubes were divided into model soils and natural subsoils. A portion of model soils collected at 10 and 386 days was stored at 4 °C before measuring soil microbial biomass C and N, dissolved organic C and N, inorganic N, and water content. The natural subsoils and a portion of model soils collected at the four sample times were air-dried for soil organic C and total N analyses. The remaining model soils collected at 386 days were stored at −80 °C for microbial community DNA extraction. To estimate necromass-derived CO2-C production, three PVC tubes of each necromass and control treatment were attached to a 1 L PVC chamber on 21 September 2018 (3 days), 28 September 2018 (10 days), 6 October 2018 (18 days), 12 October 2018 (24 days), 21 October 2018 (33 days), 28 October 2018 (40 days), 22 April 2019 (216 days) and 9 October 2019 (386 days). Then, a 150 mL gas sample was taken from each chamber at 0 h and 2 h using a syringe and stored in air bags for CO2 concentration and isotope measurement. The CO2 concentration and isotope ratio were analyzed using a CO2 isotope analyzer (CCIA-36d-EP, LGR, USA).

Physical fractionation
The model soils at day 386 were separated into four distinct OM fractions using a combined size-density fractionation protocol64. Air-dried model soil (18-20 g) was gently capillary-saturated with sodium iodide solution (NaI; 1.8 g cm−3) after 12 h, the free-floating particulate organic matter (fPOM) was collected using a vacuum pump. Occluded POM (oPOM) was released from soil aggregates by ultrasonic dispersion (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 2200; 440 J mL−1)65, enabling its separation from the heavier mineral fractions. Both fPOM and oPOM fractions were washed several times with deionized water to remove excess salt. While coarse and clay fractions were separated by wet sieving, mineral fractions < 53 µm were separated via centrifugation, and later combined as one MAOM fraction.

Necromass and soil chemical analyses
The specific surface area (SSA) of model soil materials and bulk model soils were determined by N2 adsorption at 77 K and subsequent desorption of nitrogen with a Tristar 5-point BET-instrument on freeze-dried samples. The total soil porosity was estimated from the measured bulk density and the particle density. The air-filled porosity was calculated as the difference between the total porosity and volumetric water content. The N and OC contents of the necromass and soil samples were determined by combustion using an elemental analyzer (Vario EL III; Elementar, Hanau, Germany). Inorganic N including ammonium (NH4+-N) and nitrate (NO3−-N) was extracted from fresh model soils using 2 M potassium chloride at a soil:water ratio of 1:5 and analyzed using a continuous flow injection analyzer (Autoanalyzer 3 SEAL, Bran and Luebbe, Norderstedt, Germany). The N isotope ratios of NH4+-N and NO3−-N were measured using the ammonium diffusion method 61. Microbial biomass C (MBC) and N (MBN) were determined by a fumigation-extraction method 66. Two subsamples (fumigated and non-fumigated) of fresh model soils were extracted with 0.5 M K2SO4. The non-fumigated soil extracts were used to measure dissolved organic C (DOC) and N (DON). The C and N concentrations of the extracts were determined by a TOC-500 analyzer (Shimadzu Corporation). The C or N isotope ratios of necromass C and N, soil organic C and total N, MAOM fractions, dissolved organic C and N, microbial biomass C and N, and inorganic N were analyzed using an Elementar Vario EL Cube (Elementar Analysis System GmbH) interfaced with an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (IsoPrime100, IsoPrime Limited, Stockport, UK).

To characterize the chemical composition of bacterial and fungal necromass, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analysis was performed. Briefly, freeze-dried bacterial and fungal necromass were finely ground, mixed with KBr at a ratio of 1:100 (wt:wt), and analyzed using a Thermo Nicolet 6700 infrared spectrometer (Thermo Electron Scientific Instruments Corp., Madison, WI, USA). Absorbance spectra (4000-400 cm−1) were recorded with 64 scans and a resolution of 4 cm−1. Absorbance intensity at 700, 860, and 975 cm−1 corresponded to aromatic groups; 2855, 2930, and 3300 cm−1 were assigned to aliphatic groups; and 1075 cm−1 corresponded to polysaccharide group 67. The relative absorbance intensity (rA, %) of each of the seven bands was normalized to the percent absorbance intensity of the sum of absorbance intensities of the seven bands.

To characterize the microbial community composition of bacterial and fungal necromass, PLFA analysis was performed. Briefly, 80 mg freeze-dried necromass was extracted with a chloroform:methanol:phosphorus-buffer (volume ratio: 1:2:0.8). After the organic phase was separated, dried, purified, and subjected to methyl esterification, lipids were analyzed using an Agilent 7890B GC (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) equipped with MIDI software. Microbial composition was reflected by the biomarker PLFAs of different microbial groups68.

SEM and NanoSIMS micro-spectroscopy
To directly visualize the distribution of added microbial necromass on mineral surfaces, we used SEM and NanoSIMS to analyze the model soils at 386 days. Dried model soil samples (<0.15 mm) were dispersed in deionized water, and 10 µL of the suspension was deposited onto a germanium wafer and dried overnight in a desiccator. To avoid the charging phenomena, samples were gold-coated prior to SEM analysis by physical vapor deposition under an argon atmosphere (Emitech Sputtercoater SC7620, Gala Instrumente, Bad Schwalbach, Germany). The microscale structures of mineral–necromass associations were first examined by SEM (Jeol JSM 5900LV, Freising, Germany). Representative regions were then analyzed using a Cameca NanoSIMS 50 L (Cameca, Gennevilliers, France). For NanoSIMS analysis, a high Cs+ primary ion beam current was used to remove surface contamination and gold coating, and to implant Cs+ ions into the sample to enhance the yield of secondary ions. Secondary ions of 12C−, 13C−, 12C14N−, 12C15N−, 16O−, 28Si−, and 27Al16O− were collected simultaneously using electron multipliers with a fixed dead time of 44 ns. Ion images were acquired with a dwell time of 2 ms pixel⁻¹, at a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels over a 35 × 35 µm area in a single scan cycle. For each sample, five regions of interest were analyzed to obtain a representative dataset for quantifying ¹³C and ¹⁵N distribution.

NanoSIMS image data were processed using the OpenMIMS plugin in Fiji (Schindelin et al., 2012). All images were corrected for electron multiplier dead time (44 ns). The ion images of 12C− and 12C14N− were merged for an indicator of native OM49. Regions of interest (ROIs) on these images were selected using the threshold option with the default method. All ROIs with an area greater than 10 pixels2 were used for further calculations. The 13C−:(12C− + 13C−), 12C15N−:(12C14N− + 12C15N−) ratios, and the area of the ROIs were extracted from all images and used for further calculations. The new, necromass-derived OM defined as ROIs in the 13C−:(12C− + 13C−) and 12C15N−:(12C14N− + 12C15N−) ratio image with pixel values greater than natural abundance levels.

Amplicon sequencing and data processing
Soil genomic DNA was extracted from 0.25 g freeze-dried soil collected on the last sampling time using PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kits (MoBio Laboratories, Carlsbad, CA, U.S.A.). Bacterial and fungal communities were assigned by amplifying and sequencing the V4–V5 region of the 16S rRNA gene and the ITS1 region, respectively. After PCR amplification and purification, 16S rRNA and ITS gene sequencing were performed using the Illumina platform. Raw sequences shorter than 200 bp or with a quality score below 20 (Q < 20) were removed prior to analysis using the QIIME 2 pipeline. Quality-filtered sequences of 16S rRNA and ITS gene amplicons were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% sequence similarity using UPARSE. Taxonomic classification of representative bacterial and fungal ASVs was conducted using the SILVA database and the UNITE database, respectively. Observed OTUs and phylogenetic diversity were calculated to assess microbial alpha diversity.

Data analysis
To determine the fraction of necromass-derived C or N (Cfrac or Nfrac) in the model soils, subsoil, microbial biomass, dissolved organic matter, inorganic nitrogen, and headspace gas, we calculated the fraction of each pool that was necromass-derived by the following isotope mixing model:
Cfrac or Nfrac = (atom%Sample − atom%Control) / (atom%Necromass − atom%Control) (1)
where atom%Sample is the atom% of 13C or 15N value of the C or N pools (i. e., MBC, MBN, DOC, DON, CO2-C, IN, model soil and subsoil C or N) of a given sample; atom%Control is the atom% of 13C or 15N in the equivalent C or N pool from the control; atom%Necromass is the atom% of 13C or 15N in the labelled microbial necromass added to soils.

The 13C or 15N recovery was calculated as the percentage of labelled C or N remaining in each C or N pool (MBC, MBN, DOC, DON, IN, bulk soil, and subsoil C or N) relative to initial necromass inputs. The 13C recovery in CO2-C was calculated using linear interpolation between sample points. The 13C recovery in necromass C was calculated by subtracting the 13C recovery in MBC and DOC from the 13C recovery in model soil C. The 15N recovery in necromass N was calculated by subtracting the 15N recovery in MBN, DON, and IN from the 15N recovery in model soil N.

Due to the variability and limited sampling times for 13C and 15N recovery of labelled necromass, the commonly used one- or two-pool exponential decay models could not accurately simulate our data. Therefore, we determined the mineralization rate constant of necromass 13C or 15N (kC or kN) using a linear regression on the natural log transformation of 13C or 15N recovery69.
kC or kN = ln (St / S0) / (t − t0) (2)
where St is the recovery of necromass 13C or 15N in bulk soil at the end of the experiment (t); S0 is the recovery of necromass 13C or 15N in bulk soil at the beginning of the experiment (t0).

A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to assess the effects of clay content (low-, medium- and high-clay) and microbial groups (bacteria and fungi) on the mineralization rate constant and cumulative gaseous emissions of necromass. A three-way ANOVA was conducted to assess the effects of clay contents, microbial groups, and time on necromass fates in different soil C or N pools. A repeated measures ANOVA model (MANOVA) was used to compare the effects of clay contents, microbial groups, and time on the retention and gaseous emissions of necromass. Statistical findings were considered significant if the confidence level was set at 95% (P < 0.05). The above statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 19.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Additionally, linear regressions were used to analyze the relationship between the necromass retention and bacterial community diversity (richness-B), soil moisture content, specific surface area (SSA), microbial metabolic quotient (qCO2), and air-filled porosity (AFP) at the end of incubation. Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted to explore relationships between necromass retention and environmental variables. Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) with Bray-Curtis distance was conducted to explore differences in microbial community composition using amplicon data. Statistical differences in the microbial community composition were tested using permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA). Both PCA and PCoA analyses were conducted in R (v. 4.4.3) using the vegan package70. Response: We thank the reviewer for recognizing the importance of our study and for
the insightful comments encouraging a deeper mechanistic interpretation. In response,
we conducted additional Nanoscale Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (NanoSIMS)
analyses to directly visualize clay-necromass associations, which show that newly
formed microbial necromass is preferentially associated with organic matter coatings
on rough mineral surfaces, rather than bare minerals. Complementary density
fractionation analyses further revealed that microbial necromass is predominantly
present within the mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) fraction. Together, these
results provide the first direct experimental evidence that mineral-organic matter-
necromass interactions are a key mechanism underlying the stabilization of microbial
necromass in soils. We also emphasize that while it is expected clay content will
increase necromass retention, this concept is based primarily on the binding capacity of
clay and overlooks other, potentially competing factors, that can occur in a clay-rich
environment, such as elevated decomposition associated with higher biomass, and
further does not account for other protection pathways such as reductions in leaching.

with clay content emerge as important controls on loss and retention pathways.

activity and diversity. Clay content also influences microbial community
composition32,33, which in turn shapes both necromass production and decomposition.

hydrophobic interactions, resulting in a comparable degree of organic–organic
association. We have now added these new results into the main text and discussed
these results in the context of other information in the literature.

Comment: Line 257-261: I feel that this needs more explanation and discussion – it

bacterial and fungal necromass or just the absolute rates.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. The adsorption of
microbial necromass by minerals and organic matter is a rapid process, typically
completed within seconds to hours. Previous study has also shown that in short-term
incubations (e.g., within 3 days), the majority of microbial necromass become
associated with mineral surfaces or other necromass. Accordingly, the necromass we
added would have been quickly adsorbed by minerals or organic matter. Furthermore,
our fractionation results indicate that at the end of the incubation, most of the necromass
was retained within mineral-associated organic matter (~96.4% necromass 13C and
93.4% necromass 15N), whereas only a small fraction stabilized within soil aggregate
(~1.2% necromass 13C and 2.3% necromass 15N) (Fig. S6, same as below Fig. R6). The
initially added necromass were not protected by aggregates and therefore had only a
minor influence on the experimental results. The high leaching observed in low-clay
soil is attributable to their relatively lower amount of micropores and soil surface charge
resulting from the low clay content, as evidenced by the much lower leaching rates in
high-clay soil (~7% necromass 13C and 7.5% necromass 15N) (Fig. 4). In summary,
while absolute mineralization or leaching rates may differ from field conditions, our
experimental design reliably captures the influence of clay content and necromass
source on necromass preservation. These clarifications have now been incorporated
into the revision and list as follows:
“Although our study provides clear mechanistic insights, several limitations
should be acknowledged. First, the injected necromass was not initially associated with
minerals as naturally occurring necromass would be, making a portion more susceptible
to early leaching. However, mineral adsorption appears to occur rapidly36, and
aggregate protection played only a minor role under our conditions, suggesting that this
effect did not substantially bias the overall patterns of necromass retention and
decomposition. Consistent with this, leaching in the high-clay treatment quickly
declined to low levels, with only about 7% of necromass-derived ¹³C and 7.5% of ¹⁵N
moving into the subsoil after 10 days, corresponding to a possible overestimation of the
decomposition rate constant by 0.068 and 0.073 yr⁻¹, respectively.” (Lines 261-269)

Comment: Wang et al. carried out an experiment of intermediate nature in which
synthetic soils with three different clay contents were inoculated with microbial
necromass with labelled 13C and 15N and with living microorganisms, and the synthetic
soils were placed in an experimental plot for up to one year. Intermediate times were
sampled to follow the progress of several variables. The final goal was to investigate
whether soil clay content or the type of necromass (bacterial or fungal) affected the
preservation of this necromass. The authors conclude that clay caused a significant
retention of necromass in the soil, and there is no difference between bacterial and
fungal necromass.
The goals are of great interest, the experiments are carefully designed and there are
numerous analyses to constrain the results. However, as the result analyses demonstrate,
the experimental design would have required still further care to address all the possible
pitfalls that may invalidate results. I am left with the question whether the authors
simply or mainly measured transfer of OM down the column, so that, as expected, more
OM remained where the clay content was greater; or whether their different amounts
of clay genrated a different microbial population, which modified the results of the
experiments. The discussion is poor and shows in greater contrast the limitations and
possible pitfalls of the study. In my opinion, the ms should be rejected.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for your thorough assessment and
constructive comments. We greatly appreciate the recognition that our work is well-
designed and timely, and we also acknowledge the reviewer’s concerns regarding
presentation and potential limitations in our conclusions. Below, we provide
clarifications and additional evidence addressing the reviewer’s concerns.
Our experimental system was carefully designed not only to capture the variation
in leaching, but also to disentangle the effects of adsorption processes and microbially
mediated mineralization both driven by differences in clay content on necromass
retention. Our results clearly demonstrate that necromass retention was strongly
associated with both microbial community characteristics and soil physicochemical
properties. Among these, bacterial community richness (Richness-B), soil moisture,
total porosity, specific surface area (SSA), fungal community richness (Richness-F) and
microbial metabolic quotient (qCO ) were identified as key predictors.
composition of microbial communities under different clay content and assessed how
their variations affected necromass retention. Additionally, we added new Nano-scale
Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (NanoSIMS) and density fractionation analyses to
better elucidate the role of clay content in adsorption processes. These results provide
the first direct evidence that necromass in soils is primarily preserved through
associated with organic matter already bound to these rough mineral surfaces, rather
than through directly adsorption onto the mineral surface. Soils with higher clay
contents retained more microbial necromass due to their greater abundance of rough
mineral surfaces.
Finally, we have thoroughly revised the Discussion section to provide a more
comprehensive interpretation of our findings and to explicitly address the study’s
limitations. We emphasize that these limitations have only a minor influence on our
main conclusions. We believe these revisions have substantially improved the clarity
and robustness of the manuscript.

ROUND 1 REVIEWER 1 ATTACHMENT:
This is an important study to investigate the effect of clay content on microbial necromass
persistence, in experiments conducted in situ in real soils. I think that the work is interesting to a
broad readership, but I think the authors miss an opportunity to provide new information on why
high clay content increases microbial necromass persistence. Based on previous work I feel that
the take home message that high clay content increases microbial necromass persistence is rather
expected, and the work as it stands serves as a confirmation of this expectation, rather than
providing a substantial advance in understanding of this expectation. For this reason, I think the
work as it stands is perhaps not ready for publication in Nature Communications but could be with
some extra analyses that allow the authors to more rigorously interrogate some of the speculative
explanations that they provide for their results. I have some more minor comments on the
introduction and results below, and then I exemplify my main point at several sections of the
discussion below.
Introduction:
Line 22: clay minerals are not usually described as the most reactive soil particles (metal
(oxyhydr)oxides are much more reactive and play a disproportionately important role in elemental
cycling in soils), but they are among the most reactive soil particles – so I suggest rephrasing as: “as
among the most reactive soil particles”
Line 48: adsorption not absorption
Line 50: how does soil clay content affect the living microbial community and why does this
suggest that soils with high clay content could alternatively exhibit lower necromass persistence? –
this is later explained in lines 68-82 but I feel there needs to be better connection between this
statement and the eventual explanation later on.
Line 53: do the authors mean clay minerals are characterized by their high charge and specific
surface area? (also their SSA is nowhere near as high as iron (oxyhydr)oxides, for example).
Line 97: I feel that a short description of the field experiments using model soils is warranted here
– its quite difficult in the methods to follow what was actually done – whilst the experiments were
conducted in situ in a field plot, the authors use model artificial soils, so I think that this needs to
be clearly explained – a flow diagram or some sort of schematic in the main text or supplementary
information would be really helpful to show the reader what was done (Fig 1 and Fig S8 are helpful
but two separate figures makes it difficult to follow – I feel that these could be combined).
Line 88 and 101: whilst the higher N content of bacterial necromass may also result in tighter
binding to minerals, the chitin content of fungal necromass is known to degrade into carboxyl-
containing compounds which adsorb very strongly to soil minerals, so perhaps this needs to be
considered wrt this hypothesis – at least upon its introduction around line 88.
Results:
Line 115: how much of the added C was partially mineralised (to DOC)? – I think this would be
instructive to add at this point of the results.
Line 166: this sentence doesn’t make sense – “Biochemical characterization using FTIR analyses
indicated that had a higher relative abundance of polysaccharides and a lower relative abundance
of polysaccharides compared to fungal necromass (Table S1).” – I think that Table S1 shows that
bacteria necromass has a lower abundance of polysaccharides compared to fungal necromass?
Discussion:
Line 177-198: concerning the main result that as clay content increases, a greater proportion of the
added necromass 13C and nitrogen 15N is retained in the model soil, despite the concurrent
increase in microbial biomass: whilst this may be the first study to demonstrate this outcome in
situ, which is important (at least to the extent that this is truly an in situ experiment), I think that
the outcome is to be expected based on previous work, so I feel that this work misses an
opportunity to provide new information on why this expectation holds true in situ in soils. I think
that the authors do a decent job in providing potential explanations for their result (their language
is necessarily speculative), but they are unable to pinpoint the actual explanation without
more detailed examination of the clay-necromass association. In this regard I feel that the
overarching take home message is an important one, but is rather expected, and as such the work at
the moment probably does not provide as substantial an advance in understanding as it could do.
Line 216-229: concerning the result that there was substantial leaching of necromass: did the
authors measure / approximate molecular weight of the necromass and/or measure the pore
volume of the clays? – this would provide validation of their speculative explanations.
Line 240-241: concerning the result that bacterial and fungal necromass exhibited similar
mineralization rates: this section and exemplified at the cited lines is very speculative. I feel that
this work would make a much stronger contribution to the literature if the authors provided a
more in-depth analysis of the mineral-necromass associations – the speculation that bacterial
necromass is more strongly adsorbed by minerals than fungal necromass need not be speculation
– there are many wet chemical techniques that are routinely used to operationally define strength
of adsorption that could be used here, and/or direct observational techniques, including FTIR that
the authors already employ elsewhere in the work.
Line 257-261: I feel that this needs more explanation and discussion – it was indeed one of the
issues I wanted to raise wrt the experiments. Are the experiments still relevant for evaluating in
situ mineralisation rates? Does this aspect of the experimental design affect the relative
differences between the mineralisation rates of bacterial and fungal necromass or just the
absolute rates?
